common_name: Butte Sideoats Grama (Early-Maturing Kansas-Nebraska Native Grass Selection)

planting.note: Direct sow or plant divisions in spring in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; Butte is an early-maturing, winter-hardy sideoats grama release that reliably sets seed by mid-August even in shorter-season climates.

directions: Grow Butte sideoats grama in lean, well-drained to rocky soil in full sun, where it establishes readily from either direct-sown seed or transplanted divisions. Selected for its earlier maturity relative to other regional ecotypes, Butte produces its oat-like, one-sided seed heads and completes seed development by mid-summer to early fall, making it well suited to shorter-season northern plains gardens where later-maturing selections may fail to set seed. Foliage stays fine-textured and blue-green through summer, aging to warm tan in winter for good cold-season structure. Once established it tolerates drought, heat, and poor soils with ease, and needs only an annual late-winter cutback to stay tidy.

common_name: Trailway Sideoats Grama (Late-Maturing Nebraska Native Grass Selection)

planting.note: Direct sow or plant divisions in spring in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; Trailway is a late-maturing sideoats grama release that needs most of the growing season to fully set seed, best suited to longer-season regions.

directions: Plant Trailway sideoats grama in full sun and lean, well-drained soil, either by direct seeding in spring or by setting out divisions. This Nebraska-origin release matures later in the season than other named sideoats grama selections, needing a long, warm growing season to fully develop its distinctive one-sided, oat-like seed heads, so it performs best south of the northern plains where Butte is favored instead. Slender blue-green foliage forms a dense, fine-textured clump that turns coppery tan in winter, providing season-long interest with minimal input. Highly drought- and heat-tolerant once established, it thrives in rocky or sandy soils unsuited to lusher grasses. Cut the clump back in late winter before spring growth resumes.

common_name: Niner Sideoats Grama (Southwestern Native Rangeland Grass Selection)

planting.note: Direct sow or plant divisions after soil has warmed in spring in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; Niner was selected from a Socorro, New Mexico ecotype for vigorous growth and strong palatability in the arid Southwest.

directions: Grow Niner sideoats grama in full sun and lean, fast-draining soil typical of Southwestern rangeland and gardens. Released from a vigorous Socorro, New Mexico ecotype, this selection is prized for strong seedling establishment and robust regrowth in arid, high-heat conditions, along with good palatability that made it historically important for rangeland forage as well as ornamental and restoration plantings. Fine blue-green stems bear the classic one-sided oat-like seed heads in mid-to-late summer, aging to attractive tan through winter. It tolerates extended drought and alkaline soils with ease and needs only an annual cutback in late winter to refresh the clump.
sources: New Mexico State University Cooperative Extension

common_name: Rain Dance Big Bluestem (Compact Maroon-Red Fall-Color Native Prairie Grass)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in average to moist, well-drained soil in full sun; Rain Dance is a more compact big bluestem selection with green foliage streaked crimson in summer that deepens to maroon, purple, and scarlet in fall.

directions: Site Rain Dance big bluestem in full sun in average, well-drained to slightly moist soil, where it is somewhat slow to establish but becomes reliably drought-tolerant once rooted in. This selection stays noticeably more compact and upright than the wild species, with summer foliage marked by streaks of crimson and wine-red that build to a full maroon, purple, and scarlet display by autumn, topped by the three-pronged turkey-foot seed heads typical of the species. It tolerates a range of soils, including some salt exposure, and provides persistent winter seed heads valued by seed-eating songbirds. Cut the clump to a few inches above ground in late winter before new growth begins.

common_name: Dancing Wind Big Bluestem (Dwarf Red-Fall-Color Native Prairie Grass, PP26,892)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in average to dry, well-drained soil in full sun; Dancing Wind is a dwarf, patented big bluestem selection bred by Brent Horvath as a seedling of 'Indian Warrior' with reliable scarlet fall color.

directions: Plant Dancing Wind big bluestem in full sun in average to dry, well-drained soil, where it thrives in summer heat and humidity and tolerates drought once established. Shorter and more distinctly upright than its parent 'Indian Warrior', this patented selection opens the season with yellow-green foliage accented in red, then reliably deepens to a striking deep scarlet that persists through winter, moving gracefully in the wind as the common name suggests. Turkey-foot seed heads form in fall and feed birds and small wildlife through the cold months, and the clump self-seeds readily if seed heads are left standing. Cut back in late winter or very early spring before new growth emerges to keep the clump vigorous.
